sections.title: Section 2
sections.context: A welcome talk by the leader of a community beekeeping workshop.

groups.heading: Questions 11–16
instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.stem: The speaker says beekeeping differs from other outdoor activities because

options.A: it can easily be fitted into a weekend
options.B: it involves working with a self-organising colony
options.C: the starter equipment is unusually cheap

items.stem: Inspectors sometimes identify a hive’s previous use from

options.B: the material the hive is made from
options.C: marks left on the landing board

items.stem: Some people join the class because they want to

options.A: sell honey at a local market
options.B: pass a hive on to their family
options.C: copy a neighbour who already keeps bees

items.stem: What does the speaker value most about being a beekeeper?

options.A: the calming effect of inspecting a hive
options.B: the physical work of lifting the boxes
options.C: the messy and unpredictable nature of the activity

items.stem: Most of the visitors to the apiary

options.B: are visiting for the first time
options.C: want to try advanced techniques immediately

items.stem: The speaker reminds visitors that they should

options.A: remove jewellery and tie back long hair
options.B: learn how to light the smoker before the tour
options.C: put on a veil before leaving the bench area

groups.heading: Questions 17 and 18
groups.stem: Which TWO things does the speaker explain about the smoker?

options.A: when the first version of it was invented
options.B: what the smoke actually does to the bees
options.C: where a spare smoker should be kept at home
options.D: what some beekeepers use instead of a smoker
options.E: how to repair a damaged bellows

groups.heading: Questions 19 and 20
groups.stem: Which TWO points does the speaker make about beekeeping tools?

options.A: Some have names that are difficult to remember.
options.B: Some are surprisingly heavy to hold.
options.C: Some are adapted from tools used in other trades.
options.D: Some need to be cleaned after every visit to the apiary.
options.E: Some are no longer being manufactured.

sections.title: Section 3
sections.context: Two university students discussing research for a presentation on academic burnout.

groups.heading: Questions 21 and 22
groups.stem: Which TWO things do the students both believe are responsible for the increase in academic burnout?

options.B: the growing use of social media
options.D: a recent change in term dates

groups.heading: Questions 23 and 24
groups.stem: Which TWO findings associated with burnout do the students agree are based on solid evidence?

options.B: It is a direct cause of depression.
options.C: It is linked to higher drop-out rates.

groups.heading: Questions 25 and 26
groups.stem: Which TWO opinions do both the students express about Merrow’s threshold model of burnout?

options.D: It should be more widely accepted.

groups.heading: Questions 27–30
instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.stem: When comparing burnout to ordinary stress, the students

options.A: doubt that a complete cure for burnout will ever exist
options.B: think the link between the two is overstated
options.C: express frustration that burnout is not taken seriously

items.stem: Why do the students decide to start their presentation with an example from their own experience?

options.A: to show how severe burnout can become
options.B: so the audience will recognise the situation
options.C: to illustrate a difference between men and women

items.stem: The students agree that short walks are a good strategy for dealing with burnout because

options.A: they help students generate new ideas
options.B: they interrupt the cycle before it builds
options.C: they are recommended in most study guides
